Then I get home and there’s a pile of papers from school—attendance, free lunch stuff, a note about picture day—and I just stare at it. I don’t know what I’m doing.

Money is tight. Like, I’m doing the bus, counting change, trying to make meals out of whatever is left. I’m behind on a bill and I keep thinking if I mess up at school or miss a call they’re gonna think I’m not taking care of my kid. I’ve had bad experiences with agencies before and it makes me scared to ask for help. I don’t want anybody in my business.

Can you help me figure out a simple plan for mornings? Like a routine I can actually follow when I’m tired. And maybe what to say to the school if I’m late or if I can’t make a meeting because I don’t have childcare.

Also… is there something quick I can do when I feel that spike in my chest? Like when my kid is talking and I’m nodding but I’m not really there. I hate that. I’m sorry. I just need something that works when I’m in it.

Hey AS, I’m really glad you reached out. It sounds incredibly heavy to carry all this stress, and I’m here to help with small, manageable steps.

For mornings, let’s create a simple routine to ease the rush. Start by prepping the night before—lay out clothes, pack a bag, and set a timer for 5 minutes to organize school papers. In the morning, focus on just three things: wake up, quick breakfast, and out the door. Set a single alarm 10 minutes before you need to leave as a reminder. Keep it basic; you don’t need perfection.

If you’re late or can’t make a meeting, a short, honest message works: “I’m so sorry, I couldn’t arrange childcare for today. Can we reschedule or discuss over the phone?” Most schools understand life happens.

When that chest spike hits, try a quick grounding trick: take a slow, deep breath for 4 seconds, hold for 4, and exhale for 4. Notice one thing you can feel, like your feet on the floor. It’s small but can pull you back to the moment with your kid.

I’m here if you want to talk more about any of this. You’re not alone.
